Placements.utility_in_reading: Classical geomancy treats the Judge as the court's answer. Read it first to frame the shield, then use the houses, perfections, and witnesses for detail. It states the outcome in broad terms; the rest of the chart explains how and why.
Placements.essence: The Judge is the court's verdict: the single figure formed from both witnesses, and the headline answer the chart gives.
read_when: Always, once the shield is complete and you want the court's answer to the question
First among the court figures, to frame how the rest of the shield and house chart should be read
When the question asks chiefly whether something will happen, fail, wait, or resolve with qualification
After weighing Right and Left Witness to see which side the verdict favors
Before turning to houses for detail, perfections, or the Way of Points
pitfalls: Skipping the Judge and letting the house chart alone stand in for the court's verdict
Discarding the Judge because a single house figure tells a prettier story
Forgetting that only even figures can be Judge; odd arithmetic means the shield was built incorrectly
examples: Judge Acquisitio from Albus and Caput: the deal or course is profitable overall, though the witnesses named different parts of the case
Judge Populus: the outcome follows allies, rumor, or collective movement; check the Eleventh house for detail

meaning: How the Judge's verdict combines with the querent

Whether the querent can accept, bear, or prosper under the outcome the Judge names
Placements.utility_in_reading: The Reconciler does not replace the Judge. It is Judge plus First House, so it translates the court's verdict into personal terms: what that answer will mean for this querent once it lands. When it repeats the Judge, the outcome and its personal effect are of one piece.
Placements.essence: The Reconciler joins the Judge to the First House: how the verdict sits on the querent, and what it will mean for them in practice.
read_when: After the Judge, when you need the personal effect of the verdict on the querent
When the querent asks what this means for me, not only whether it will happen
When Judge and Reconciler show different figures or tones, so reception, cost, or relief becomes part of the reading
When Judge and Reconciler repeat the same figure, to show the outcome will land on the querent directly without softening or extra burden
When the First house is central to the question and you need to see the verdict combined with the querent's own significator
pitfalls: Treating the Reconciler as a second verdict that can overturn the Judge
Reading it before the Judge, when it has no meaning without the court's answer
Missing repetition with the Judge; the same figure in both places usually means the outcome will stick as stated
examples: Judge Laetitia with Reconciler Carcer: the answer is favorable, but the querent will soon feel bound by new structure or obligation
Judge and Reconciler both Fortuna Major: the outcome is favorable and the querent can actually live with and benefit from it
Judge Fortuna Major with Reconciler Tristitia: success arrives, but with private heaviness or regret for the querent
